details:
**Amu Darya and Syr Darya**
The two rivers that fed the Aral Sea: the Amu Darya (the ancient Oxus) from the south and the Syr Darya (the ancient Jaxartes) from the northeast. Starting around 1960, Soviet planners diverted so much of their water for irrigation that the sea began to shrink dramatically.

**Karakum (Qaraqum) Canal and Soviet cotton farming**
One of the world's longest irrigation canals, it takes water from the Amu Darya across Turkmenistan's Karakum Desert to grow cotton. The canal is unlined and leaky, losing a huge share of its water to seepage and evaporation, and it was a chief cause of the Aral's drying.

**Vozrozhdeniya (Rebirth) Island**
An island in the Aral that was a secret Soviet biological weapons testing site. Its now-abandoned town of Kantubek housed the facility, and anthrax was buried there in large quantities. As the sea receded, the island joined the mainland, raising fears that pathogens could spread.

**1971 Aralsk smallpox outbreak**
An outbreak of smallpox in the port town of Aralsk in 1971 that killed three people. It is widely believed to have come from a weaponized strain tested on Vozrozhdeniya Island.

**Moynaq (Muynak) ship graveyard**
A former fishing port in Uzbekistan whose fleet was stranded far from water as the sea retreated, leaving rusting ships on the dry seabed. Its population and fishing industry collapsed. The decline of Aral fishing is the subject of the 2012 film Waiting for the Sea.

**Once the fourth-largest lake in the world**
Before 1960 the Aral Sea was the world's fourth-largest lake. It has since lost the large majority of its area and volume (over 80%) and split into a Northern (Small) Aral in Kazakhstan and a Southern (Large) Aral, often called one of the worst human-made environmental disasters.

**Kok-Aral Dam (Dike Kokaral)**
A dike across the Berg Strait, completed in 2005 with World Bank funding. It separates the Northern Aral from the southern basin and holds Syr Darya water in the north, letting that part's water level, salinity and fisheries recover.

**Drying of the eastern basin**
The Southern Aral itself split into western and eastern lobes. The eastern basin dried out completely in 2014, leaving the new Aralkum Desert, whose salty, chemical-laden dust storms harm people's health.

**Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan border**
The Aral Sea straddles the border between Kazakhstan to the north and Uzbekistan to the south, in the Turan Lowland of Central Asia, with the Kyzylkum Desert to its southeast.

**Karakalpakstan and Nukus**
The autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan in Uzbekistan lies south of the sea, around the Amu Darya delta, and has suffered most from the disaster. Its capital is Nukus, and Moynaq is also in the region.

**Aralsk (Aral)**
The sea's namesake port city in Kazakhstan, once on the northern shore. It is now stranded many kilometers from the water.

**"Sea of islands"**
The name "Aral" comes from a Turkic word for "island," and the lake is often described as the "sea of islands" because it once held more than a thousand islands. It is a geologically young basin that formed in the late Neogene.
